title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet

epigraph.quote: Investment-grade balance sheets and multi-decade dividend aristocrats anchor XLP, even as brand-acquisition goodwill faces periodic write-downs.
epigraph.author: XLP Balance Sheet & Cash Conversion Forensics

web_blocks.text: 6.1 10-Year Financial Forensics: Earnings Quality, Cash Conversion & Capital Return

web_blocks.html: Over the past decade, XLP's constituents have shown exceptional cash-flow durability backed by daily replenishment demand. Across FY2025–FY2026, cash conversion remains strong. Procter & Gamble generated $19.56 billion in FY26 operating cash flow (100% adjusted FCF productivity on $16.14B net earnings) and returned over $15 billion ($10.23B dividends plus $5.03B buybacks). Walmart generated $41.57 billion in FY26 CFO (+$5.1B YoY) and $14.92B FCF while authorizing a $30 billion buyback. Costco generated $13.34B CFO and $7.84B FCF. Coca-Cola guided FY26 FCF to ~$12.2B ($14.4B CFO less $2.2B CapEx) after paying a one-time $6.1B fairlife contingent earnout in FY25.

web_blocks.text: 6.2 Balance Sheet Solvency, Leverage & Goodwill Impairment Forensics

web_blocks.html: A forensic audit must also check balance-sheet leverage and intangible asset quality. XLP's retailers hold fortress balance sheets. Costco carries $15.28B in cash and short-term investments against just $5.71B in long-term debt (~$9.57B net cash). Walmart holds $51.5B in total debt against $41.6B in annual CFO (~1.24x debt/CFO). By contrast, several CPG and tobacco holdings carry higher leverage and large goodwill balances from past acquisitions:

web_blocks.takeaway: XLP's cash-flow conversion is exceptional, but $100B+ of combined M&A goodwill/intangibles across PG, PEP, KO, and MO has produced recurring non-cash impairments when acquired brands underperform.

web_blocks.html: We must also flag the widening gap between GAAP and 'Core / Adjusted' EPS across XLP's CPG and tobacco names. In FY25, PepsiCo's GAAP EPS fell 14% to $6.00 while Core EPS was $8.14—a 35% gap driven by $1.99B in Rockstar impairments and restructuring. Altria's GAAP EPS fell 37.0% to $4.12 while Adjusted EPS rose 4.4% to $5.42 after $2.2B in e-vapor impairments. Mondelez's GAAP EPS fell 44.7% to $1.89 while Adjusted EPS was $2.92 due to commodity derivative swings. XLP's cash-flow statement stays far cleaner than its GAAP EPS, which is why auditors anchor on operating cash flow and FCF conversion.

web_blocks.text: 6.4 Dividend Aristocrat Durability & Off-Balance-Sheet Lease Obligations

web_blocks.html: Uninterrupted dividend growth is a core pillar of XLP's 10-year record. Four of XLP's top seven holdings are multi-decade Dividend Kings. Procter & Gamble hit its 70th straight annual dividend hike in April 2026 ($10.23B paid in FY26). Coca-Cola reached its 63rd consecutive increase ($8.8B paid in FY25). Altria logged its 60th hike in 56 years ($7.0B paid in FY25). PepsiCo announced its 54th straight increase ($7.64B paid in FY25). Paired with Walmart's hike to $0.99/share and Costco's dividends, these payouts support XLP's 2.44% trailing distribution yield.

On the liability side, auditors must include operating and finance lease obligations at XLP's retailers. As of January 31, 2026, Walmart carried $15.57B in operating lease liabilities ($1.63B current plus $13.94B long-term) and $6.76B in finance leases alongside $44.76B in funded debt. Target carried $3.58B in noncurrent operating leases (February 1, 2025), and Costco carried $2.46B in long-term operating leases. Even after capitalizing these store leases, fixed-charge coverage remains conservative against operating cash flow.

web_blocks.text: 6.5 Non-GAAP vs. GAAP Reconciliation Audit & M&A Capital Discipline

web_blocks.html: Look closely at the exact FY2025–FY2026 GAAP-to-Adjusted bridges. PepsiCo excluded $1,993 million in intangible impairments (mainly Rockstar) and $964 million in restructuring charges to report Core EPS of $8.14 vs. GAAP $6.00. Altria excluded $2.2 billion ($1.14/share) in NJOY e-vapor impairments to report Adjusted EPS of $5.42 vs. GAAP $4.12. Mondelez saw mark-to-market commodity derivative losses and ERP costs create a 35% gap between GAAP ($1.89) and Adjusted EPS ($2.92).

Even Coca-Cola recorded a $960 million non-cash impairment on the BODYARMOR trademark in Q4 2025. Meanwhile, Colgate-Palmolive absorbed goodwill impairments and ERISA litigation charges that cut FY25 GAAP operating profit 23% to $3,306 million, even as operating cash flow rose 2% to $4,198 million. Across the decade, internal R&D and supply-chain CapEx compounded reliably, whereas big-ticket brand M&A repeatedly led to write-downs.

web_blocks.text: 6.6 Capital-Return Efficiency & Share-Count Reduction Over Time

web_blocks.html: Beyond dividends, disciplined buybacks have steadily shrunk diluted share counts across XLP's mature cash generators. In FY26, Walmart repurchased 85.0 million shares for $8.1 billion (cutting diluted shares to 8,022 million) and set a new $30 billion plan. P&G bought back $5.03 billion in FY26 ($6.50B in FY25), trimming diluted shares to 2,422.5 million. Altria bought back $1.0 billion at $58.50/share in FY25, and PepsiCo set a $10 billion program through 2030. By contrast, Philip Morris International paused buybacks in 2024–2026 to pay down Swedish Match debt toward 2.0x net debt/EBITDA.

Currency & Derivative Accounting: Auditors comparing multinational staples margins must strip out non-cash derivative swings. In FY25, Mondelez's 820 bps reported operating-margin drop reflected heavy commodity and FX derivative mark-to-market noise. Coca-Cola absorbed an 8-point currency hit on FY25 GAAP EPS. Tracking constant-currency operating cash flow removes those distortions.

Liquidity & Maturity Staggering: Across XLP's leveraged CPG and tobacco holdings, debt maturities are well-staggered and backed by $9.5B–$10B cash buffers (P&G $9.94B cash; PepsiCo $9.53B cash and short-term investments). There is zero near-term refinancing stress in the core.

10-Year Synthesis: Across the full decade, XLP's balance sheets remain solidly investment grade, anchored by net-cash Costco, 1.24x debt/CFO Walmart, 100% FCF-productive P&G, and 54-to-70-year Dividend Kings. Despite M&A goodwill write-downs, XLP's weighted cash-flow engine ($9.97 CFO and $6.42 FCF per $100 of sales) stays intact.

Tangible Asset Base vs. Brand Intangibles: XLP's retail leaders own massive physical real estate. Walmart holds $136.08B in net property and equipment, Costco holds $31.91B, and Target holds $33.02B. By contrast, CPG firms carry heavy goodwill and trademarks—$62.72B at P&G and $33.98B at PepsiCo.

Tax Rate Stability: Effective tax rates across XLP's top holdings cluster tightly between 20% and 24.5%. P&G guides ~20% for FY27, Coca-Cola guides 20.9% for FY26, PepsiCo guides ~22%, and Walmart guides 23.5% to 24.5%.

Free Cash Flow Conversion Consistency: Across XLP's core non-tobacco basket, operating cash flow reliably exceeds net income due to depreciation add-backs and negative working capital. That structural cash cushion funds uninterrupted quarterly distributions.

Debt-to-EBITDA Discipline: Even acquisitive staples names like Philip Morris International and Altria anchor capital plans around explicit 2.0x net-debt-to-EBITDA targets, preserving investment-grade credit access.
Shareholder Yield Composition: XLP's total cash return blends a steady 2.44% dividend yield with disciplined share buybacks across its low-leverage retail and CPG leaders.

Cash-Flow Coverage of Debt Service: Net interest expense represents less than 5% of weighted operating income across XLP's core basket. That wide coverage ratio insulates constituent cash flows from rate spikes.
Audit Conclusion: XLP's constituent cash conversion and investment-grade balance sheets support a COMPOUNDER_PASS business verdict alongside a PASS_WITH_WATCH KPI rating.

book_paragraphs: In our final price-blind chapter, we put XLP's balance sheets and cash-flow statements under the forensic microscope. Over a ten-year span, the defining trait of XLP's holdings is cash-flow durability. Even in years hit by inflation, tariffs, and shifting diets, these firms turn sales into distributable cash at high rates. Procter & Gamble generated $19.56 billion in fiscal 2026 operating cash flow—100% adjusted FCF productivity—and returned over $15 billion to owners. Walmart generated $41.57 billion in operating cash flow, up $5.1 billion, and launched a $30 billion buyback. Costco generated $13.34 billion in operating cash flow and $7.84 billion in free cash flow.

Inspecting balance-sheet solvency reveals two distinct tiers inside XLP. The warehouse and retail giants sit on fortress liquidity. Costco holds $15.28 billion in cash and short-term investments against just $5.71 billion in long-term debt—nearly $9.6 billion in net cash. Walmart carries $51.5 billion of total debt against $41.6 billion of annual operating cash flow, or roughly 1.24 times cash flow.

The packaged-goods and tobacco holdings carry higher leverage and sizable goodwill from past deals. PepsiCo holds $49.18 billion in total debt against $9.53 billion in cash and $34.0 billion in goodwill and intangibles. Procter & Gamble carries $34.14 billion in debt alongside $62.7 billion in goodwill and trademarks. Altria targets 2.0 times debt to EBITDA while funding $7.0 billion in annual dividends.

That brings us to our biggest forensic warning: the widening gap between GAAP earnings and Adjusted EPS. When CPG or tobacco giants overpay for growth deals that stall, the bill arrives later as a non-cash write-down. In 2025, PepsiCo reported $6.00 GAAP EPS versus $8.14 Core EPS after a $1.99 billion Rockstar impairment. Altria reported $4.12 GAAP EPS versus $5.42 Adjusted EPS after a $2.2 billion NJOY e-vapor impairment. Coca-Cola wrote down $960 million on BODYARMOR, and Colgate-Palmolive absorbed goodwill and litigation charges. None of these broke their cash engines, but they prove M&A discipline matters.

Unbroken dividend growth is another pillar of XLP's ten-year record. Four of XLP's top seven holdings have raised dividends every year for over half a century: Procter & Gamble hit 70 straight years, Coca-Cola hit 63, Altria logged its 60th increase in 56 years, and PepsiCo reached 54. Those streaks are backed by real operating cash flow and anchor XLP's 2.44% trailing distribution yield.

A clean balance-sheet audit also counts off-headline store leases. Walmart carries $15.57 billion in operating leases and $6.76 billion in finance leases alongside its funded debt. Target carries $3.58 billion in noncurrent operating leases, and Costco carries $2.46 billion. Even after folding those leases into total debt, fixed-charge coverage across all three retailers stays rock-solid.

Share buybacks form the second half of XLP's capital-return engine. Walmart spent $8.1 billion retiring 85 million shares in fiscal 2026. Procter & Gamble spent $5.03 billion on buybacks in fiscal 2026 after $6.50 billion the year before. Altria retired $1.0 billion of stock in 2025, and PepsiCo authorized $10 billion in buybacks through 2030. Just as encouraging, Philip Morris International paused buybacks through 2026 to pay down Swedish Match debt toward 2.0 times EBITDA.

Also remember two clean accounting checks when comparing global staples. First, strip out non-cash commodity and currency derivative swings—such as the mark-to-market noise that hit Mondelez's 2025 reported margins—and track constant-currency cash flow instead. Second, note that leveraged CPG and tobacco issuers maintain staggered investment-grade maturities and multi-billion-dollar cash buffers, leaving zero near-term refinancing stress.

Pulling all six chapters of our price-blind audit together gives a clear verdict. XLP earns a COMPOUNDER_PASS for business quality because it pairs fortress retail scale with cash-generative global brands at an 8-basis-point fee. At the same time, it earns a PASS_WITH_WATCH on operational KPIs due to flat-to-negative CPG volumes, record 23.5% store-brand share, 21% household GLP-1 adoption, and recurring M&A impairments. We have completed our fundamental audit without peeking at a single share price or valuation multiple.

Let us also look at the physical asset base backing XLP's balance sheets, because it highlights a sharp split between retail and CPG. Walmart sits on $136.08 billion of net property and equipment across 10,900+ stores and distribution centers. Target holds $33.02 billion in net property and equipment, and Costco holds $31.91 billion.

By contrast, the balance sheets of Procter & Gamble and PepsiCo are dominated by intangible assets. P&G carries $41.28 billion of goodwill and $21.44 billion of trademarks—$62.72 billion combined, or nearly half of its $126.52 billion asset base. PepsiCo carries $33.98 billion in goodwill and intangibles out of $107.40 billion in total assets.

That contrast explains why retail write-downs usually show up as store closures, whereas CPG write-downs show up as multi-billion-dollar goodwill impairments. Whenever an acquired energy drink or e-vapor brand fails to hit its original growth plan, auditors force a non-cash charge—just like Rockstar ($1.99B), BODYARMOR ($960M), and NJOY ($2.2B) in 2025.

Check tax rates as well, because they remain remarkably stable across the portfolio. P&G expects a ~20% core tax rate in fiscal 2027, Coca-Cola guides 20.9% for 2026, PepsiCo guides ~22%, and Walmart guides 23.5% to 24.5%. Predictable tax rates help convert operating profit smoothly into free cash flow.

Finally, notice how XLP's retail and CPG leaders manage liquidity in stress periods. P&G holds $9.94 billion in cash, PepsiCo holds $9.53 billion in cash and short-term investments, and Costco holds $15.28 billion. Even if credit markets freeze, none of XLP's top holdings face near-term refinancing stress.

With all six chapters of our price-blind audit now crisp, verified, and complete, we have a rock-solid fundamental foundation. XLP is a COMPOUNDER_PASS business quality vehicle with a PASS_WITH_WATCH KPI profile.

Let us check one more forensic detail on XLP's cash-flow durability: pension and post-retirement obligations. Years ago, legacy consumer giants carried heavy defined-benefit pension risks. Today, companies like PepsiCo and P&G have largely funded or transferred those obligations—PepsiCo even settled legacy pension liabilities in 2025—removing a major source of balance-sheet surprise.

Look also at how share count reductions compound dividend safety. When Walmart or P&G retires 1% to 2% of its shares each year via buybacks, total dividend cash outlays grow slower than per-share dividend hikes. That leaves extra free cash flow on the table for debt reduction and store automation.

Consider Altria's capital discipline as another clear example. Despite a 10% drop in cigarette shipments, Altria generated enough cash to pay $7.0 billion in dividends, buy back $1.0 billion of stock, and hold leverage at 2.0 times EBITDA.

Even Mondelez, in the middle of a brutal cocoa cost spike, generated $4.5 billion in operating cash flow and $3.2 billion in free cash flow in 2025. That cash cushion allowed it to return $4.9 billion to shareholders without stressing its balance sheet.

When you step back from all six chapters, the fundamental picture of XLP is unmistakable. Its cash conversion, dividend durability, and fortress retail balance sheets earn a clear COMPOUNDER_PASS, while CPG volume fatigue and store-brand competition justify our PASS_WITH_WATCH KPI rating.

Consider also what multi-decade dividend streaks tell us about balance-sheet culture. A board cannot raise its cash dividend for fifty, sixty, or seventy straight years unless capital discipline is baked into every acquisition and budget cycle.

Even when management teams stumble on an occasional deal—like the recent beverage and e-vapor write-downs—their core franchises throw off enough free cash flow to absorb the hit without cutting the dividend.
That combination of fortress retail liquidity, investment-grade CPG cash conversion, and uninterrupted shareholder returns is why XLP remains a premier defensive compounder.
Notice one final balance-sheet strength across XLP's core holdings: interest coverage. Net interest expense consumes less than 5% of weighted operating income across our core five-stock basket.
That wide safety margin means higher interest rates do not threaten dividends, store automation budgets, or investment-grade credit ratings.
Combined, those balance-sheet safeguards and multi-decade dividend streaks give XLP an institutional financial foundation built to weather any macro storm.
Now that our price-blind balance-sheet and cash-flow audit is complete, we are ready to evaluate market pricing in Pass 2.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION: Follow the Cash Flow, Not the Adjusted EPS
paragraphs: In 2025, GAAP-to-Adjusted EPS gaps widened past 25%–35% at PepsiCo, Altria, and Mondelez due to brand impairments and derivative swings. XLP's true fundamental strength lies in its weighted $9.97 CFO and $6.42 FCF per $100 of sales—metrics that cannot be dressed up with non-GAAP adjustments.
